translations: Aman was perched on a stone by the riverbank, scribbling away. When he heard the comment, his hand twitched and his old brush left a black dot right next to the “Lotus‑Lotus‑Root Avatar.” He looked up at the sky and said, “I don’t know if it’s leaking rain or not, but if you keep using the Hunyuan Silk to bathe, the Chen Tang Pass will definitely start leaking.” Nezha tried to take a couple of steps, but his right foot went wonky and almost caught the hem of his own robe. He straightened up at once, “Just grew these legs, still learning the way.” Aman nodded seriously, “I’ll write that down so you don’t blame the ground when you fall again.” Nezha plucked a lotus petal and stuck it on Aman’s forehead, “Then you wear one too, so the old brush doesn’t lose its hair to the wind.” They gave each other a quick stare, and Lady Yin finally burst out laughing.

Nezha’s steps were like a frog just out of a mud pit—wobbly and unsteady, his toe tips constantly snagging on the edge of his robe, as if an invisible hand were gently nudging him. Aman’s brush tip danced across the bamboo slip, trembling a bit whenever Nezha’s slight wobble made the page shake, so the characters slanted like an impromptu poem. Nezha lifted his head, squinting at the distant sky as if searching for a path that would steady his footing. Aman rested his pen lightly on his shoulder, as if giving himself a little boost, muttering, “Don’t let that path turn into a slide.” Nezha grinned, then pressed the lotus petal onto his own forehead, crowning himself with a tiny flower—playful and cute.

On Aman’s green bamboo slip, besides the black dot beside “Lotus‑Lotus‑Root Avatar,” a few lines read, “Nezha’s steps are unsteady; more practice needed.” Lady Yin stood nearby, cradling a bowl of cool tea, glancing up at Nezha now and then with a mix of worry and a hint of relief. Nezha gently shook the Hunyuan Silk onto the ground, turning his little “bath” routine into a theatrical performance. Aman glanced at the sky and whispered, “If you keep using the Hunyuan Silk as swimwear, the water at Chen Tang Pass will rise with you.” Nezha laughed, as if saying, “Then let it rise a bit—surprise everyone!” Lady Yin couldn’t help but laugh, and the whole riverside instantly felt light and cheerful.

When the East Sea surged again, Nezha marched out of the city with the Lotus‑Lotus‑Root Avatar in tow. Ao Guang transformed into a black dragon coiling over the waves, still demanding that Chen Tang Pass pay for Ao Bing’s life. Nezha didn’t retreat, nor did he let Taiyi Zhenren or his parents step forward. He flung the Hunyuan Silk, wrapping the dragon’s horns in crimson ribbons; Ao Guang thrashed his tail, raising a wall of water, and Nezha leapt on the crest, striking the dragon’s claws with the Qiankun Ring. The magical tools were the same old ones, but their wielder no longer fought just for a quick thrill. Whenever a massive wave barreled toward the villagers, Nezha first split the surf to shield the shore, then turned to face Ao Guang. After a back‑and‑forth, Ao Guang became bound by the Hunyuan Silk, the Qiankun Ring hanging before him, unable to flood the city any longer.

Nezha didn’t take his life; he said, “I’ve already repaid Li Gen and Ao Bing with my own life. If you still want to vent on the people, I’ll block you again.” Seeing the villagers retreat to higher ground and spotting Li Jing and Lady Yin behind Nezha, Ao Guang finally cooled his anger. He conceded and withdrew the water. The waves receded layer by layer back into the East Sea, and the roofs, fields, and docks of Chen Tang Pass reappeared. Nezha personally subdued the Dragon King and halted the flood, but he didn’t brag about the victory—he simply turned to help right the door panels that the water had knocked askew.

After the water went down, Nezha didn’t rush home. A gate panel on East Street was jammed in a stone ditch, so he and a few carpenters lifted it out; the salt‑field drainage ditch was clogged with seaweed, and he rolled up his pant legs to clear it until dusk darkened the sky; a small fishing boat sat stuck on the dock steps, and ten people couldn’t budge it. Nezha tied the Hunyuan Silk to the boat’s bow, but first asked the old boatman how to tie the knot. The boatman, surprised that Nezha actually asked, deliberately slowed down, “First call me ‘Master.’” Nezha stared, “My master would swap bodies with lotus roots—can you do that?” The boatman patted the hull, “I only know how to keep a boat from falling apart, and today you need that.” Nezha thought a moment and finally called out, “Old master!” Everyone laughed, and together they pushed the boat back into the water. Aman recorded everything, and when he wrote “Nezha listened to advice,” he stopped his brush and read it three times, fearing the sea might have given him a hallucination. Nezha snatched the slip, “Write those three characters bigger.” Aman protected the green bamboo slip, “Rare things should be written small, so they don’t fill the whole page and leave no room to note the next mishap you cause.” Nezha stubbornly claimed he wouldn’t cause any more trouble, but the Hunyuan Silk snagged an empty bucket at his feet, clanged loudly, and the whole street heard the crash.
